course.learn: This section focuses on **Significance** within **Power**. Power resilience is significant because electricity failures can cause downtime, data corruption, hardware damage, and violations of availability commitments. Power planning is therefore part of cybersecurity resilience.
course.why: Critical services depend on stable power before any software security control can function.
course.example: A UPS prevents abrupt shutdown during a short outage, while generators support longer operation so an SLA can still be met.
course.exam: Power questions usually connect to availability, UPS, generators, graceful shutdown, redundancy, and environmental risk.

course.learn: A generator provides longer-duration backup electricity when utility power fails, typically after a short startup delay.
course.why: Critical facilities may need to operate through extended outages that batteries alone cannot cover.
course.example: A data center UPS carries the load for a few seconds while diesel generators start and take over.
course.exam: Generator = sustained backup power. UPS = immediate short-term power/conditioning.

defs: Uninterruptible Power Supply: provides immediate short-term power during an outage or power-quality event.

course.learn: An Uninterruptible Power Supply (UPS) provides immediate battery-backed power and often power conditioning during short outages or while a generator starts.
course.why: It prevents sudden shutdowns, gives systems time to fail over, or allows a graceful shutdown.
course.example: When utility power drops, servers continue running on UPS batteries until the generator reaches stable output.
course.exam: UPS = immediate/short term. Generator = longer duration.
